title: Strong El Niño to Intensify From August, Adding Fuel to 'a Planet Already on Fire'
excerpt: The World Meteorological Organization warns El Niño will steadily strengthen through October, combining with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole to amplify drought, floods, and heatwave risks worldwide.
body:
• The WMO warns a strong El Niño will intensify during August–October 2026, raising global temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns across continents.
  • A simultaneous positive Indian Ocean Dipole is forecast, amplifying drought, flood, and wildfire risks around the Indian Ocean basin — including India, where the weakest monsoon in 11 years is already under way.
  • UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the phenomenon "fuel to a planet already on fire," warning of scorching heat domes, apocalyptic wildfires, and record-hot seas.

The United Nations weather agency warned on Friday that a strong El Niño is expected to intensify starting in August, with the warming of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean set to steadily build into a powerful event through October 2026. The World Meteorological Organization said the phenomenon is likely to push global temperatures further above normal and dramatically shift rainfall patterns across multiple continents.

The warning marks the third escalation of WMO forecasts since June, when the agency first confirmed El Niño's onset with an 80% probability. By early July, climate scientists said there was "remarkable agreement between forecast models" that conditions would reach the strong category — the third-highest on the WMO's four-tier scale. Seasonal-average sea-surface temperature anomalies are now expected to exceed 2°C in key Pacific monitoring regions.

"El Niño is strengthening — adding fuel to a planet already on fire with scorching heat domes, apocalyptic wildfires and record hot seas. Fossil fuels are fanning the flames of this crisis."

— António Guterres, UN Secretary-General

A Compound Climate Threat

The WMO flagged an additional concern: a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is forecast alongside the strengthening El Niño. The IOD, a climate pattern in which the western Indian Ocean warms while the eastern Indian Ocean cools, can compound regional impacts when it coincides with El Niño. Together, the two phenomena amplify drought, floods, and wildfire risk — particularly around the Indian Ocean basin, according to the agency.

The combination is not theoretical. WMO climate scientist Alvaro Silva said El Niño's effects will be felt "in different regions until the end of the year and beyond, also during 2027." The last El Niño in 2023–24, one of the five strongest on record, played a direct role in making 2024 the hottest year ever recorded, at roughly 1.55°C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial average.

Already, the consequences are materialising. Europe endured its worst recorded heatwave between June 20 and 28, disrupting power generation, damaging infrastructure, and overwhelming healthcare systems. Peru declared a 60-day state of emergency across 800 of its 1,800 municipalities over the "imminent danger" of heavy rains and flooding linked to El Niño, putting more than 9.3 million people on alert.

India Faces a Weakened Monsoon

For India and its diaspora, the stakes are acute. The India Meteorological Department has warned that this year's southwest monsoon is tracking at 90% of its long-period average — the weakest since 2015. The monsoon delivers roughly 70% of India's annual rainfall and underpins an agricultural sector that employs nearly half of the country's 1.5 billion people and accounts for about 18% of its nearly $4 trillion economy.

Economists are warning of inflation pressures. "A deficient monsoon, particularly in the crucial July–August months, can push inflation closer to 5.5% if food inflation spikes," said Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at IDFC First Bank, according to Reuters. India's retail inflation stood at 3.48% in April, but the outlook is clouded by energy costs linked to the Middle East conflict.

Weak rainfall could shrink harvests of rice, cotton, and soybeans, and reduce soil moisture for winter crops like wheat. India — the world's largest rice exporter and second-largest sugar producer — has previously restricted grain exports during El Niño years, as it did in 2023. Hot weather is already hurting Asian crop planting from India's northwestern plains to Indonesia's palm oil plantations, with wheat and rice prices climbing 20% and 15%, respectively, since the start of 2026.

What's Next

The WMO said it is intensifying its mobilisation of information and support services to help countries anticipate and minimise impacts. WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said 128 countries now have multihazard early warning systems in place, with the UN targeting universal coverage by the end of 2027.

"We need to prepare for a potentially strong El Niño event, which will exacerbate drought and heavy rainfall and increase the risk of heatwaves both on land and in the ocean."

— Celeste Saulo, WMO Secretary-General

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is forecasting an 81% chance of a very strong — or "super" — El Niño through the October-to-December period, potentially placing it among the most powerful events on record since 1950. Should conditions escalate further, the WMO has said it could revise its classification upward. For now, the agency's message to governments is unambiguous: prepare.
nri_angle: India faces its weakest monsoon in 11 years as El Niño suppresses rainfall, threatening food prices, crop exports, and inflation — key concerns for the Indian diaspora watching economic conditions back home.
author: Diaspora Desk
